paragraphs.heading: A ribbon of sand offshore
paragraphs.text: A barrier island is a strip of sand lying off the coast and running parallel to the mainland. Waves and tides build it, and it counts as a kind of dune system and sand island. These islands usually come in long, narrow chains, which can run for hundreds of kilometers with tidal inlets cutting between the islands. The longest one in the world is Padre Island in Texas, at 182 km.

paragraphs.heading: A shield for the coast
paragraphs.text: Barrier islands protect the coast. They soak up the energy of incoming waves, and behind them they create sheltered waters where wetlands can thrive. A breakwater is a structure people build offshore, parallel to the shore, and it has the same effect: it weakens the waves and currents hitting the coast, just as a natural barrier island does. Each island is part of a linked coastal system that trades sediment and energy among its parts, so a change in one part can affect the whole.

paragraphs.heading: Always reshaping
paragraphs.text: A barrier island is never fixed. Waves, tides, moving sediment and changes in sea level make it shift, grow or wear away over time. If an important inlet closes for good, an island can turn into a barrier peninsula. Barrier beaches and spits are close relatives that look alike, but they differ mainly in how firmly they are tied to the mainland and whether water lies on their landward side. Tidal range, wave energy, sediment supply and sea-level trends all shape a barrier's size and form, and the plants growing on it strongly affect how tall it gets and how it changes.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: About 1,500 barrier islands have been identified worldwide, with a combined length of more than 15,000 kilometers. Chains of them line roughly 13 to 15% of the world's coasts. Most are in the northern hemisphere: North America has more than a third of them and Asia close to a quarter. They turn up in many different settings, which suggests they can form and last in a range of environments, and many theories have been put forward to explain how they form.

paragraphs.heading: From the sea to the beach
paragraphs.text: Seen from the ocean side, an island has distinct zones. The shoreface is where the ocean reaches the island's shore, and the island body separates it from the backshore and the lagoon behind. The foreshore is the land between high and low tide. Waves work on it all the time, and their crashing energy leaves coarser sand, very well sorted, with cross-bedding and fine layers.

paragraphs.heading: Dunes and the lagoon behind
paragraphs.text: The backshore always sits above the highest water level, and the berm marks where it meets the foreshore. Here wind matters more than water, though big storms can bring in or strip away sand. Wind builds coastal dunes along the top of the backshore, and unlike ordinary wind-blown dunes they hold the roots of coastal plants and marks left by sea life. These dunes also help the island grow. Behind them lies a lagoon and tidal flat, where the water is still enough for fine silt, sand and mud to settle.
